sections.h2: Where is the Greene County Recorder of Deeds, and when can I visit?
sections.html:
The Recorder of Deeds sits at 940 N Boonville Ave in Springfield, MO 65802, and the main line is (417) 868-4068. The county lists Cheryl Dawson-Spaulding as Recorder. Counter hours run Monday through Friday, 8:00 am to 4:30 pm, with holidays excluded.

The same building holds the Greene County Assessor, in Room 35 at (417) 868-4101. A seller who needs a parcel's legal description for a deed can walk down the hall instead of driving across town. The assessor's Public Access site also lists ownership, taxing district and school district for each parcel, and the county says the data refreshes every night.

sections.h2: What does the Greene County recorder actually record?
sections.html:
The office keeps the public record of real property in the county, so every deed, deed of trust, release and easement for a Greene County house ends up there. Missouri law ties your deed to this office: RSMo 442.380 says an instrument that conveys real estate is recorded with the recorder of the county where the land lies.

Besides land records, the county page lists these duties:

  • Recording and keeping records that concern real property
  • Issuing and keeping marriage license information
  • Filing and keeping federal and state tax liens
  • Filing and keeping military discharges

The recorder does not draft anything. Per the county FAQ, a title company or an attorney prepares any new document that changes ownership.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to record a deed in Greene County?
sections.html:
The county fee schedule charges $26.00 for the first page of a real estate document and $3.00 for each added page. Send a postage-paid envelope, or add postage to your payment, if you want the recorded original mailed back.

Greene County Recorder of Deeds fee schedule (greenecountymo.gov/recorder/fees.php)

A banner on the recorder page announces that Senate Bill 938 raises the fee for real estate documents, plats and surveys by $2 as of August 28, 2026. That date is behind us, so call the office for the amount it charges today. State law also adds a user fee on every instrument: RSMo 59.319 sets it at six dollars, collected on top of other recording fees.

sections.h2: What format must a Greene County deed follow before it is accepted?
sections.html:
Under RSMo 59.310, a recorder may refuse papers that miss the layout rules. A document that does not conform can still be recorded for an extra $25 fee, so a clean first draft saves money. The main rules:

  • Pages printed on one side only, not bound, in black or dark ink, with type no smaller than eight point
  • White or light paper of at least twenty-pound weight
  • A top margin of at least three inches for the recorder's stamp, and three-quarter inch margins elsewhere
  • On the first page below that margin: the title, the date, grantor names and marital status, grantee names, any statutory addresses and the legal description

Section 59.330 adds two more items. A deed needs a legal description, and every deed other than an easement or right-of-way needs a mailing address for at least one grantee. A rejected document comes back to the person who presented it, along with the reason.

sections.h2: What is the recording deadline each day, and what about the sale price?
sections.html:
The county's recording time policy stops intake at 4:00 PM on business days. Anyone standing at the counter by 4:00 PM gets the day's recording. Papers that arrive later are recorded starting at 8:00 AM the next business day, and the policy asks you to leave staff time to check the pages.

On price, the county FAQ states that the selling price of real estate is not required on recorded deeds, and the fee schedule above has no transfer tax line. Your title company will tell you if anything else is due at closing.

sections.h2: How do I look up a recorded document or a lien on a Greene County house?
sections.html:
The office cannot search by street address. It needs a full legal description, a book and page, a name or a document number. A seller with only an address should get the legal description from the Greene County Assessor first.

The recorder is barred by law from running lien searches, and it says it is not the only office where liens on property are filed. The staff will help you search the records yourself. A subscription service offers raw data downloads, but it does not show document images on the website. For a sale, the title company runs the full lien and ownership check.

sections.h2: What should a Greene County seller know about the local housing picture?
sections.html:
Greene County covers 678 square miles in southwest Missouri, and Springfield is the county seat and largest city. The Census Bureau estimated 309,286 residents on July 1, 2025, up from 298,915 in the 2020 count, which Wikipedia lists as the most populous county outside the Kansas City and St. Louis areas.

  • Housing units: 142,405, with 130,951 households in 2020 to 2024
  • Owner-occupied share: 57.5%
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $221,300
  • Median gross rent: $989
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 966

Beyond Springfield, the county's cities include Ash Grove, Battlefield, Fair Grove, Republic, Rogersville, Strafford, Walnut Grove and Willard. School districts named for county towns include Springfield R-XII, Republic R-III, Logan-Rogersville R-VIII, Ash Grove R-IV and Fair Grove R-X, so the district on your deed's parcel record can matter to buyers. Major routes are I-44, US 60, US 65 and US 160.

sections.h2: How does recording fit into selling a Greene County house?
sections.html:
Recording is the last step of a sale. After closing, the signed deed goes to 940 N Boonville Ave, and the recorder stamps it into the public record for Greene County. The assessor then updates its tax maps from the warranty deeds it receives from the recorder, which is how a new owner's name and parcel lines show up in the county's parcel data.

Plan the paperwork before you list. If a name on title has changed, or a relative who owned the home has died, a new document must be prepared to change ownership, and the county says a title company or an attorney may assist, because the recorder's office does not prepare documents. Ask your closing agent to check the legal description, the grantee mailing address and the margins against the rules above a few days before you sign.

faqs.q: Does Greene County charge a transfer tax when I record a deed?
faqs.a: The county fee schedule lists no transfer tax, and the recorder's FAQ says the selling price is not required on a recorded deed. You pay the recording fee by page count. Ask your title company about any other closing charges.

faqs.q: What time should I get a deed to the Greene County recorder?
faqs.a: Be at the counter by 4:00 PM on a business day. The county policy accepts nothing after that hour, and later papers are recorded from 8:00 AM the next business day.

faqs.q: Can the Greene County recorder find out whether my house has liens?
faqs.a: No. The office is prohibited by law from conducting lien searches and notes that liens are filed in more than one office. Staff can help you search the records, and your title company runs the formal check before closing.

faqs.q: How do I find the legal description for my Greene County property?
faqs.a: Ask the Greene County Assessor at 940 N Boonville Ave, Room 35, or use the assessor's Public Access site. The recorder's index needs a legal description, book and page, name or document number rather than a street address.

faqs.q: What happens if my deed does not meet the recorder's format rules?
faqs.a: The recorder may refuse it and return it with a reason. Under RSMo 59.310 a nonconforming document can instead be recorded for an extra $25 fee.
